extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, district and appellate judges, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_short: IPR estoppel analysis in patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for applying 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) IPR estoppel, and related procedural and appellate-review rules in post‑IPR district-court patent litigation. Includes when estoppel bars invalidity defenses, how SAS/Caltech affect scope, and standards for summary judgment and leave-to-amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner in an inter partes review of a claim in a patent that results in a final written decision under section 318(a) (or the real party in interest or privy) may not assert in a civil action that the claim is invalid on any ground that the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised during that inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory text (35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2)) is the starting point: estoppel bars asserting invalidity in later civil actions on grounds raised or that reasonably could have been raised in the IPR that resulted in a final written decision. The existence of a final written decision is a prerequisite to triggering the estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim application of § 315(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR estoppel applies on a claim-by-claim basis; the statute refers to 'a claim in a patent' and 'the claim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel is assessed with respect to particular patent claims. Relevant authorities (e.g., Intuitive, Caltech) analyze estoppel at the claim level rather than globally across a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition defines the scope of IPR post-SAS
rubrics_metrics.description: After SAS, 'the petitioner's contentions, not the Director's discretion, define the scope of the litigation all the way from institution through to conclusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because SAS rejected the Board's partial-institution practice, the IPR scope is defined by the petition's contentions. Thus, whether grounds/claims were 'instituted' is less determinative for estoppel than whether they were included in the petition and could have been considered under the petition-defined scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Reasonably could have raised" standard
rubrics_metrics.description: § 315(e)(2) bars later assertion of any ground that the petitioner 'raised or reasonably could have raised' during the IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This language means that estoppel can reach beyond the specific grounds actually decided by the Board to include grounds that the petitioner could reasonably have asserted against claims included in its petition — particularly after SAS established that the petition, not partial institution, defines the litigation's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaw (pre-SAS) principle regarding denied grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Shaw, grounds denied by the Board at institution were treated as never becoming part of the IPR and therefore were not subject to IPR estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shaw held that a ground rejected at institution 'never became part of the IPR' and thus could not trigger estoppel; the opinion here explains that Caltech and SAS have undermined Shaw's rationale and that Shaw is no longer controlling in the post-SAS context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final written decision prerequisite for estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR estoppel applies only where the inter partes review 'results in a final written decision under section 318(a)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the IPR does not culminate in a final written decision (e.g., if the petition is denied entirely or the proceeding does not produce a final written decision), § 315(e)(2) estoppel does not attach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failing to seek SAS remand
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a petitioner had an opportunity post-SAS to seek remand to have non-instituted grounds considered but did not, that failure does not shield the petitioner from estoppel as to claims included in its petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an IPR appeal was pending when SAS issued and the petitioner could have sought a remand to have the Board consider non-instituted grounds (but did not), courts may treat the petitioner's inaction as not avoiding estoppel; petitioner is not 'helpless' where remand was available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between IPR estoppel and common-law issue preclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR estoppel under § 315(e)(2) is statutory and does not require the 'actually litigated' or 'fully and vigorously litigated' prerequisites of common-law issue preclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will not graft issue-preclusion's 'actually litigated' requirement onto statutory IPR estoppel. The statute's 'reasonably could have raised' language provides a different, broader basis for estoppel than issue preclusion's litigation-focused test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for appellate review of summary judgment (regional circuit law)
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant of summary judgment is reviewed according to the law of the regional circuit (here, the Fifth Circuit) which reviews de novo; summary judgment is improper where there is a genuine dispute of material fact and a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party (Anderson v. Liberty Lobby).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a district court's summary-judgment decision in patent cases, apply the regional-circuit's standard (Fifth Circuit: de novo) and Anderson's 'genuine dispute of material fact' test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for reviewing statutory interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of statutes, including the IPR estoppel statute, is a question of law reviewed de novo by the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts review statutory interpretation without deference to the lower court's legal conclusions (citing Intuitive Surgical, Caltech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review standard for district-court procedural matters (abuse of discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: District-court decisions on procedural matters in patent cases, such as granting leave to amend claim selections, are reviewed for an abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts give deference to district courts' case-management decisions (citing O2 Micro, Mayeaux, S&W Enterprises) and will reverse only for clear abuse of that discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause requirement and timeliness for amending asserted claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A party seeking to amend its asserted claim selection long after initial selection and after a prolonged stay must show 'good cause' to reopen selection; unexplained multi-year delay weighs against amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to request amendment during long stays or promptly after IPR conclusion, combined with minimal supporting justification, is a valid basis for the district court to deny leave to amend; courts 'generally refuse to reopen what has been decided previously.'

rubrics_metrics.name: S&W Enterprises factors must be presented by movant
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking leave to amend, a movant should present and analyze the S&W Enterprises factors; the district court need not sua sponte apply that framework if the movant fails to raise it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A terse or cursory request that does not cite or meaningfully engage S&W Enterprises factors gives the district court a reasonable basis to deny amendment and the appellate court will not apply those factors de novo for the first time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition inclusion of a claim can trigger estoppel even if Board did not address it
rubrics_metrics.description: If a petitioner included a claim (and relevant grounds) in its IPR petition and the IPR otherwise resulted in a final written decision, the petition's inclusion of that claim and related references (e.g., Dezonno) can support estoppel even if the Board did not specifically decide that claim due to partial institution practices later invalidated by SAS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under SAS and Caltech, because the petition defines the scope, a petitioner who included a claim in its petition cannot avoid estoppel merely because the Board's partial-institution decision left that claim unaddressed — particularly where the petitioner could have sought a SAS remand and did not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of long stays and lack of timely communication with the court
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive delays (e.g., multi-year stays) and failure to timely notify the district court or request amendments during the stay are factors that support the district court's denial of late-in-time procedural requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party's inaction during a long stay (six-plus years in this case) and its minimal, late request to amend are legitimate bases for the district court to find lack of good cause and to exercise docket-management discretion to deny amendment.
